Field studies of the White-rumped munia (Lonchura striata) have provided detailed measurements of its early ontogeny. Eggs are typically incubated for an average of 14 days [ab = 14 days] before hatching, a developmental period that is strongly influenced by ambient temperature; under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant 32 °C [T = 32 °C], this incubation duration is highly consistent. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings are remarkably small, with an initial wet body mass of just 0.95 grams [Ww0 = 0.95 grams]. This low mass at emergence is typical for estrildid finches and reflects a strategy of producing relatively undeveloped young that are heavily dependent on biparental provisioning during the early nestling phase. The subsequent growth trajectory is rapid, with the downy chicks gaining weight steadily through the brooding period.

The developmental milestones of nestlings have been carefully documented under thermoneutral conditions maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which corresponds to the species' typical active metabolic body temperature. At this stable thermal regime, the altricial chicks achieve fledging at 23 days after hatching [tx = 23 days after hatching], a point marked by the maturation of their flight feathers and the first achievement of sustained flight at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short nestling period is characteristic of many small-bodied passerines and allows for the production of multiple broods within a single breeding season. During the later stages of this period, the developing chicks begin to exhibit exploratory behavior at the nest rim.

Reproductive investment in this species is characterized by moderate fecundity and a flexible breeding schedule. Females lay between 3 and 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 6 eggs per clutch], a value consistent with the typical range for small tropical finches, and they are capable of producing up to 2 clutches annually [F_R_i = up to 2 clutches annually] when conditions are favorable. This reproductive strategy, which allows for a maximum of roughly two nesting attempts per year, is shaped by the seasonal availability of grass seeds, their primary dietary resource. The ability to double-brood is particularly advantageous in regions with protracted wet seasons. Such a rate of offspring production contributes to the species' successful colonization of both its native Asian range and introduced island populations.

Sexual maturation and the timing of first reproduction show clear patterns under standardized thermal conditions. At a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], female White-rumped munias reach gonadal maturity at 69 days after hatching [tp = 69 days after hatching], a surprisingly early onset of reproductive capability for a passerine of this body size. However, the age at which these young birds actually initiate their first breeding attempt is considerably later. Under the same thermal regime, the time since birth at first successful brood is typically around 307 days after hatching [tR = around 307 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the energetic demands of establishing a territory and completing body growth before committing to reproduction at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

Longevity and metabolic rate data provide further insight into the species' life-history pace. Under controlled captive conditions maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 2628 days [am = approximately 2628 days], a relatively extended duration for a twelve-gram bird that reflects low extrinsic mortality in a protected environment. Basal metabolic measurements at this same thermoneutral body temperature reveal two distinct values for maximum resting oxygen consumption: a lower rate of 33.2 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 33.2 milliliters of oxygen per hour] and a higher value of 38.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 38.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This variation likely reflects differences in individual body condition or recent feeding history. The ultimate wet body weight attained by fully grown females is 12.3 grams [Wwi = 12.3 grams], a mass that falls within the broader species range of 9.5 to 13 grams.
